blocks.text: Sulfuric acid is called the king of chemicals, and its consumption is an indicator of a country's industrial progress.

items: The major portion of the acid is used to make fertilisers; normally 77.67 per cent digests phosphate rock containing calcium phosphate, Ca3(PO4)2. Fluorapatite, Ca5(PO4)3F, is treated to make single superphosphate Ca(H2PO4)2 and phosphoric acid H3PO4, which is used for double and triple superphosphates and ammonium phosphate; the acid also reacts with ammonia to give ammonium sulfate fertiliser.
Extraction of metals from ores such as Cu, Ni and steel.
A catalyst in oil and coal refining and in the polymer, synthetic rubber and plastics industries.
The pulp and paper industry, and the production of pesticides, insecticides, herbicides, varnishes, dyes, pharmaceuticals, soaps and detergents.
Nitration for explosives such as trinitrotoluene (TNT), nitroglycerine, picric acid and nitrocellulose.
The food industry, for sugar, starch and corn syrup.
The paint industry, for titanium dioxide pigment.
Lead storage batteries (35.67 per cent of the acid, as printed).

blocks.text: Although it is used in many industries, sulfuric acid is rarely contained in the final product.

blocks.prompt: Why is the consumption of sulfuric acid taken as an index of industrial development?
blocks.explanation: Almost every manufacturing sector uses it somewhere, from fertilisers and metals to paper, plastics, dyes, explosives, food processing and batteries, even though it rarely appears in the final product; so the more industry a country has, the more sulfuric acid it consumes.

items: King of chemicals: fertilisers (phosphate rock to superphosphates and H3PO4; ammonium sulfate), metal extraction, catalyst in refining and polymers, paper, pesticides, dyes, drugs, detergents, explosives (TNT), sugar and starch, TiO2 pigment, drying gases, lead batteries, lab reagent; rarely in the final product.
